name: Choi implanter pen

lead: The Choi implanter pen is a hand-held tool used in some hair transplants to open the recipient site and insert a follicular unit in one step. It is the basis of the technique marketed as DHI, aimed at fuller hair in thinning areas.

Clinics say it gives control of the angle, direction and depth of each graft and shortens the time grafts spend outside the body. Reference sources note higher cost, longer procedures and fewer grafts per session, and no controlled trial comparing the pen with other placement methods was found.

paras: Follicular units are extracted individually as in FUE, loaded into the hollow pen and implanted directly without pre-made slits. Results depend heavily on the surgeon.
Risks are those of FUE hair transplantation generally, such as swelling, folliculitis, scarring and poor graft take.

angle.text: The Choi implanter pen is the tool behind DHI, placing each follicular unit in a single step to fill in thinning areas with control over angle and depth. Clinics promote its precision, and published comparisons with other methods are absent.

lead: The Choi implanter pen is a hand-held device used in hair transplantation to make the recipient-site opening and place a harvested follicular unit in a single step. It is most often associated with the technique marketed as Direct Hair Implantation (DHI), described as a variant of follicular unit extraction (FUE) in which grafts are loaded into the pen rather than placed into pre-cut slits.[1]

Clinics that offer pen-based implantation say it gives control over the angle, direction and depth of each graft and shortens the time grafts spend outside the body. Reference sources describe the approach as typically more expensive and slower than conventional FUE, with fewer grafts per session and results that depend heavily on the surgeon.[1] The Wikipedia article on hair transplantation does not cover the pen itself, and no controlled trial comparing pen implantation with other placement methods was identified in the sources reviewed.[2]

paras: In pen-based implantation, individual follicular units are extracted by FUE and then loaded into a hollow needle-tipped pen. The surgeon uses the pen to open the recipient site and deposit the graft in one motion, so no separate slits are made in advance.[1]

Proponents cite precise control of angle and depth for natural-looking hairlines and reported graft survival above 90 to 95 percent because handling time is short.[1] Listed drawbacks are higher cost, long sessions (6 to 10 hours is cited), dependence on operator skill and fewer grafts per session.[1] These figures come from a general reference page rather than from published trials.
